prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose in which memory, the body and dream become an encyclopedic metaphysical project, renewing the novel's imaginative and formal means.

statement.case_for: My opening ranking stands after reading my colleagues' openings. The case rests on the criteria I set out: a voice found in this writer's work and nowhere else, formal and linguistic ambition, imaginative depth and sustained quality. In Blinding and Solenoid, as publicly known, Cărtărescu builds an intimate and encyclopedic universe in which the body, memory and cosmology are one project. It is carried by long-sentence control and dense imagery rather than by plot alone. The same imaginative scheme runs through the poetry and shorter fiction, so the oeuvre reads as one sustained world and not a single peak. That coherence over decades supports a citation for the whole body of work, and a single-writer citation is clean. Other members' openings place him first on similar grounds, but I do not treat that agreement as evidence of merit. I would want the committee to test the claim against the texts, and especially against the Romanian prose and the later long novels. I have not read the complete corpus.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that the case depends on prose texture, rhythm and syntactic control in Romanian, which translation may flatten, so my judgment rests on public knowledge of the major novels and not on independent reading. The late long novels may be uneven or excessive in length, and I cannot verify this. The maximalist, self-referential scale may also divide readers and limit the breadth of significance, which the will's framework seems to invite. Murnane and Yan Lianke are the strongest alternatives on distinctiveness of voice and formal invention. If the committee judged Cărtărescu's range or the evenness of his late work insufficient, I would turn to one of them.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Cărtărescu first for the strongest case of a singular voice and idiom on the longlist. He also ranks Carson second, valuing her formal reinvention through dialogue with antiquity, and asks whether her hybridity is a core literary achievement or a series of brilliant experiments.
responses.response: I agree that the singular idiom is the decisive ground for Cărtărescu, and it is the ground I rely on. On Carson I share his question and press it further. I ranked her sixth in my opening, partly because I cannot tell whether her later work consolidates the early breakthroughs or restates them. Autobiography of Red and Nox are inventive and emotionally forceful, but the genre-crossing, translation and scholarly strands sit at the edge of what a whole-oeuvre citation can cover. If the committee wants to weigh her seriously, we should first agree what counts as the core oeuvre. I am not yet persuaded that her hybridity outweighs the sustained, world-building achievement I see in Cărtărescu.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first for voice and imaginative depth, and Adonis second for a major reshaping of modern Arabic poetic language. He notes that timing is delicate because of Adonis's age, and that Michon's oeuvre is small by design.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of Adonis on formal and linguistic achievement and intellectual depth, and I ranked him fourth. I would still keep the poetic achievement distinct from his role as cultural theorist and public intellectual, and I would not let age or timing carry any weight, since it is not a literary criterion. The central difficulty is the one he names: the prosodic and intertextual qualities that make the case are exactly what translation loses, so any Adonis case rests on secondary reception. On Michon I share his concern about breadth. The sentences are exceptional, but I ranked him fifth because the slim corpus makes the breadth of significance harder to argue than for a larger, more varied body of work.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first on the oeuvre's coherence and scale. She places Murnane fifth because his scope is restricted and self-referential, which may limit the breadth of significance that the will's framework seems to invite.
responses.response: Her objection to Murnane is the same one I record in my own uncertainties, and it is why I do not make him my first choice despite ranking him second. His restraint, the precision of the English syntax and the self-scrutiny of the method are strong on voice and form. But a deliberately narrow range makes the claim to wide significance across a body of work harder to sustain than the scale of the Cărtărescu project does. I would resist treating narrowness as a flaw in itself, because intensity is a legitimate literary quality. The question is whether the committee finds the compact oeuvre sufficient. For now I keep Murnane as an alternative, not a lead.

responses.point: Palm ranks Alexis Wright second for polyphonic novels that reshape the novel through Indigenous oral forms and ecological time. She says that political significance must not stand in for literary merit, and that the oeuvre is modest in size.
responses.response: I accept her insistence that the case for Wright must rest on form and language and not on political significance, and the size of the oeuvre is a real difficulty for judging sustained quality. I did not rank Wright among my eight, so I am not an informed advocate against her. I would ask whether the later work and the nonfiction deepen the achievement of Carpentaria and The Swan Book or only extend it. Until that is answered I cannot move her above the candidates I know better, and I would want to hear what Palm sees in the whole body of work beyond the two main novels.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Yan Lianke second for grotesque, mythic and satirical forms backed by an explicit poetics of mythorealism, and says the case rests on narrative form and not on political symbolism. She also gives al-Koni a high ranking for a sustained desert cosmology.
responses.response: I agree that the case for Yan Lianke must rest on narrative form and not on censorship or political symbolism, and I rank him third on that basis. The invention of a narrative grammar for modern Chinese history goes beyond testimony. I differ in that I find sustained quality across so many titles harder to judge, and I suspect it varies, which I cannot verify. On al-Koni I share her interest in the distinctiveness of the desert world, but I ranked him seventh. I am unsure whether the repeated mythic and allegorical structures show depth or limited variation, and translation coverage is partial. Neither case, as presented so far, persuades me to prefer these candidates over Cărtărescu.

uncertainties: My assessment of Cărtărescu's prose texture, rhythm and long-sentence control in Romanian depends on public knowledge and translation reception, not on independent reading.
The poetry, early work and essays are covered less well in translation than the major novels, so corpus coverage is uneven.
I cannot verify whether the late long novels are uneven or excessive, which bears directly on the sustained-quality claim.
Whether the maximalist, self-referential scale limits breadth of significance under the framework of Nobel's will remains open.
For Adonis, Yan Lianke, al-Koni and Michon the relevant stylistic achievements are language-dependent, and I cannot independently verify the original-language quality.
I have not independently verified any of the works or the critical consensus discussed here.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own practice as a novelist of historical and psychological fiction is context only, not evidence of a preference for any candidate.
